concepts.def: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the two bonded atoms. The shared pair lies between the nuclei and attracts both of them, which holds the atoms together. It is this attraction, not any 'need' of the atoms, that constitutes the bond.

The octet rule describes the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell containing a total of eight electrons when they form bonds. It is a tendency, not a law: hydrogen is stable with two valence electrons, and atoms such as boron in BF₃ and beryllium in BeCl₂ form stable molecules with fewer than eight.

A Lewis formula (also called an electron dot or Lewis structure) shows all the valence electrons in a covalently bonded species: the bonding pairs and the non-bonding (lone) pairs. Electron pairs may be shown as dots, crosses or dashes. For an ion, the formula is placed in square brackets with the charge outside. Example: in H₂O, oxygen has two bonding pairs (one to each H) and two lone pairs, eight valence electrons in all.

A bonding pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. A lone pair (non-bonding pair) is a pair of valence electrons held by one atom and not shared. The number of electrons around an atom in a Lewis formula is found by counting both: two for each bonding pair it takes part in and two for each lone pair it holds. In NH₃, nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair (8 electrons).

Some atoms form stable molecules with fewer than eight valence electrons. Boron has three valence electrons, so in BF₃ and BCl₃ it forms three single bonds and has six electrons; beryllium has two, so in a gaseous BeCl₂ molecule it forms two single bonds and has four. These molecules are examples of atoms that do not reach an octet.

A single bond is one shared pair of electrons, a double bond two shared pairs and a triple bond three shared pairs between the same two atoms. Examples: C–C in ethane (CH₃CH₃), C=C in ethene (CH₂=CH₂), C≡C in ethyne (HC≡CH), and N≡N in N₂.

The distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, usually given in picometres (pm; 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m). For bonds between the same two atoms, bond length decreases as the number of shared pairs increases, because more shared electrons between the nuclei attract both nuclei more strongly and pull them closer: C–C 154 pm, C=C 134 pm, C≡C 120 pm.

The strength of a covalent bond is measured by its bond enthalpy, the energy needed to break one mole of that bond in gaseous molecules, in kJ mol⁻¹. For bonds between the same two atoms, strength increases with the number of shared pairs: average bond enthalpies C–C 346, C=C 614 and C≡C 839 kJ mol⁻¹. More bonds between two atoms means a shorter, stronger bond.

A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom (the donor), which must have a lone pair; the other atom (the acceptor) must be able to accept a pair. Examples: in NH₄⁺, N of NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺; in H₃O⁺, O of H₂O donates a lone pair to H⁺; in CO, one of the three shared pairs comes wholly from O; in Al₂Cl₆, a lone pair on a bridging Cl atom of each AlCl₃ unit is donated to the Al atom of the other unit. Once formed, a coordination bond is identical to any other covalent bond between the same atoms: the four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are indistinguishable.

An electron domain is a region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair, a single bond, a double bond or a triple bond each count as ONE electron domain. CO₂ has two electron domains around carbon (two double bonds); H₂CO has three; NH₃ has four (three bonding pairs and one lone pair).

The valence shell electron pair repulsion model predicts shapes from the idea that the electron domains around a central atom repel each other and take up positions as far apart as possible. Two domains: linear, 180° (CO₂, BeCl₂). Three: trigonal planar, 120° (BF₃). Four: tetrahedral, 109.5° (CH₄).

The electron-domain geometry is the arrangement of all the electron domains, including lone pairs, around the central atom. The molecular geometry (shape) describes the positions of the atoms only. They are the same when there are no lone pairs. NH₃: electron-domain geometry tetrahedral, molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal. H₂O: electron-domain geometry tetrahedral, molecular geometry bent (V-shaped).

concepts.term: Effect of lone pairs and multiple bonds on bond angles
concepts.def: Lone pairs are held closer to the central atom than bonding pairs and repel more strongly, so each lone pair reduces the angle between bonding pairs: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ about 107°, H₂O about 104.5°. A double or triple bond contains more electron density than a single bond and also repels more strongly: in methanal, H₂CO, the H–C–H angle is slightly less than 120° (about 116°).

The ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. Values on the Pauling scale include H 2.2, B 2.0, C 2.6, N 3.0, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2, S 2.6 and Cl 3.2. Electronegativity has no units.

A covalent bond is polar when the bonded atoms differ in electronegativity: the shared pair is drawn towards the more electronegative atom, which gains a partial negative charge (δ−), leaving a partial positive charge (δ+) on the other. The larger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond. A bond dipole can be shown with partial charges (Hδ+–Clδ−) or with a vector arrow pointing towards the more electronegative atom. Bonds between identical atoms (Cl–Cl) or atoms of equal electronegativity are non-polar.

A molecule is polar if it has a net dipole moment, which is the vector sum of its bond dipoles. It depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry. Bond dipoles cancel when they are equal and arranged symmetrically: CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar) and CCl₄ (tetrahedral) have polar bonds but no net dipole. They do not cancel in H₂O (bent), NH₃ (trigonal pyramidal) or CH₂Cl₂ (tetrahedral with unequal bonds), which are polar.

A giant structure in which every atom is joined to its neighbours by covalent bonds that extend throughout the solid, with no separate molecules. Melting or subliming it requires many strong covalent bonds to be broken, so network solids have very high melting points and are insoluble in water. Carbon (diamond, graphite, graphene) and silicon (silicon, silicon dioxide) form covalent network structures.

Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state. The allotropes of carbon (diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes) have different bonding and structural patterns, so they have different chemical and physical properties.

Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others arranged tetrahedrally, forming a rigid three-dimensional network. All four valence electrons of every atom are used in localized bonds, so diamond does not conduct electricity. It is extremely hard and has a very high melting point, because melting requires many strong C–C covalent bonds to be broken.

Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others in flat layers of hexagonal rings. The fourth valence electron of each atom is delocalized across the layer, so graphite conducts electricity along the layers. The layers are held together only by London (dispersion) forces, so they slide over each other easily and graphite is soft and slippery. Its melting point is very high because the covalent bonds within the layers must be broken.

A single layer of graphite: a sheet one atom thick in which each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others in hexagonal rings. It has delocalized electrons, so it is an excellent electrical conductor, and it is very strong and has a very high melting point because of its network of covalent bonds.

Fullerenes are molecular allotropes of carbon. C₆₀ is a closed cage of 60 carbon atoms arranged in 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, each atom bonded to three others. C₆₀ is a simple molecular substance: the molecules are held together by London (dispersion) forces, so it has a much lower sublimation temperature than diamond or graphite and dissolves in non-polar solvents such as methylbenzene.

Silicon has the same structure as diamond: each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral three-dimensional network. It has a high melting point (1414 °C), lower than that of diamond because Si–Si bonds are longer and weaker than C–C bonds. Silicon is a semiconductor, not a metal.

Silicon dioxide (quartz, SiO₂) is a covalent network in which each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms arranged tetrahedrally and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms. The formula SiO₂ gives the ratio of atoms; there are no SiO₂ molecules. It has a high melting point (about 1700 °C), is hard, is insoluble in water and does not conduct electricity.

Attractive forces between molecules, as opposed to the covalent bonds within a molecule. Their nature depends on the size and polarity of the molecules. They are much weaker than covalent bonds, and they are what is overcome when a simple molecular substance melts or boils.

Attractions between instantaneous dipoles and the dipoles they induce in neighbouring molecules. The electron cloud of any molecule fluctuates, creating a temporary dipole. London forces act between all molecules, polar or non-polar, and increase with the number of electrons (and so with molar mass) and with the surface area of contact.

Attractions between a molecule with a permanent dipole and a neighbouring molecule in which that dipole induces a temporary dipole. They act, for example, between an HCl molecule (polar) and an I₂ molecule (non-polar), alongside London forces.

Attractions between the permanent dipoles of neighbouring polar molecules, the δ+ end of one attracting the δ− end of another. They act, for example, between propanone molecules and between CH₃Cl molecules, in addition to London forces.

An intermolecular attraction that occurs when a hydrogen atom, covalently bonded to an electronegative atom (N, O or F), is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule. In methanol, CH₃OH, the H of an O–H group in one molecule is attracted to an O atom of another. The H atoms of the CH₃ group, bonded to carbon, do not form hydrogen bonds.
The inclusive term for dipole–dipole, dipole–induced dipole and London (dispersion) forces. Hydrogen bonding is treated separately and is not included in this term.

For molecules of comparable molar mass, the relative strengths are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding. Example: propane (M_r 44.11, London forces only, boiling point −42 °C) < ethanal (M_r 44.06, dipole–dipole, 20 °C) < ethanol (M_r 46.08, hydrogen bonding, 78 °C).

Volatility is the tendency of a substance to evaporate. Simple molecular substances are volatile, with low melting and boiling points, because only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds within the molecules do not break. Covalent network substances are not volatile, because melting them requires strong covalent bonds to be broken.

Conduction requires mobile charged particles. Simple molecular substances do not conduct as solids or liquids, because their molecules are neutral and their electrons are held in localized bonds and lone pairs. Among network substances, graphite and graphene conduct because they have delocalized electrons; diamond and silicon dioxide do not.

A covalent substance dissolves in a solvent when the attractions formed between solute and solvent molecules are comparable in strength to those broken within each. Substances whose molecules can hydrogen bond with water (ethanol, glucose) are soluble in water; non-polar substances (hexane, iodine) dissolve in non-polar solvents but not in water. Covalent network substances are insoluble in all common solvents.

A technique that separates the components of a mixture according to their relative attractions, involving intermolecular forces, to a stationary phase and a mobile phase. A component attracted more strongly to the stationary phase, relative to the mobile phase, moves more slowly and travels a shorter distance.

The stationary phase does not move (in paper chromatography, the paper, whose cellulose fibres hold water). The mobile phase (the solvent) moves through or over the stationary phase, carrying the components with it to different extents.

RF = distance moved by the component (from the baseline to the centre of its spot) ÷ distance moved by the solvent (from the baseline to the solvent front). Both distances are measured from the baseline where the sample was applied. RF has no units, lies between 0 and 1, and is characteristic of a component for a given stationary phase, solvent and temperature, so it can be compared with the RF of known substances to identify a component.

When more than one Lewis formula can be drawn for a species, differing only in the position of a double bond (and so of the electrons), these are resonance structures. The real species is a single resonance hybrid, not any one of the structures and not a mixture of them. Examples: O₃ (two structures), NO₃⁻ and CO₃²⁻ (three each), carboxylate ions such as ethanoate, CH₃COO⁻ (two).

Delocalization describes electrons that are shared among more than two atoms rather than confined to the region between two nuclei. In a resonance hybrid the electrons of the 'moving' double bond are delocalized over all the positions it could occupy, so the bonds concerned are identical and intermediate between single and double: in NO₃⁻ all three N–O bonds are identical, and in O₃ both O–O bonds are identical. Delocalization lowers the energy of the species.

concepts.term: Structure of benzene and its evidence
concepts.def: Benzene, C₆H₆, is a planar ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen atom and to two carbon atoms by σ bonds, with six π electrons delocalized around the ring. Physical evidence: all six C–C bonds are the same length, about 140 pm, between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm); the enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene (about −208 kJ mol⁻¹) is much less exothermic than the −360 kJ mol⁻¹ predicted from three times that of cyclohexene (about −120 kJ mol⁻¹), so benzene is about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than a structure with three localized C=C bonds. Chemical evidence: benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition, which keeps the stable delocalized ring intact.

Atoms of elements in period 3 and beyond (such as P, S, Cl, Br, Xe) can have more than eight electrons in their valence shell, forming five or six electron domains around the central atom: PCl₅ has five bonding pairs, SF₆ has six. Period 2 atoms (C, N, O, F) cannot expand their octet.

Five domains adopt a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry: three equatorial positions at 120° to each other and two axial positions at 90° to the equatorial plane. Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions. PCl₅ (5 bonding pairs): trigonal bipyramidal. SF₄ (4 bonding, 1 lone pair): see-saw. ClF₃ (3 bonding, 2 lone pairs): T-shaped. XeF₂ (2 bonding, 3 lone pairs): linear.

Six domains adopt an octahedral electron-domain geometry with all angles 90°. SF₆ (6 bonding pairs): octahedral. BrF₅ (5 bonding, 1 lone pair): square pyramidal. XeF₄ (4 bonding, 2 lone pairs, placed opposite each other): square planar.

The charge an atom would have if all bonding electrons were shared equally: FC = V − N − ½B, where V is the number of valence electrons of the free atom, N the number of non-bonding electrons on the atom and B the number of bonding electrons around it. The formal charges in a species add up to its overall charge. Formal charge is a bookkeeping device and differs from oxidation state, which assigns all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom.

Where several Lewis formulas can be drawn, the preferred one has formal charges as close to zero as possible. If formal charges cannot be avoided, the preferred formula places any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. Example: for CO₂, O=C=O (all formal charges zero) is preferred to O≡C–O (formal charges +1, 0, −1).

A covalent bond formed by the head-on (end-to-end) combination of atomic orbitals, so that the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis between the two nuclei. It can form from s–s, s–p, p–p or hybrid-orbital overlap. Every single bond is a σ bond.

A covalent bond formed by the lateral (sideways) combination of two p orbitals, so that the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis (above and below it) with none on the axis itself. A π bond forms only between atoms already joined by a σ bond.

concepts.term: σ and π bonds in multiple bonds
concepts.def: A single bond is one σ bond; a double bond is one σ bond and one π bond; a triple bond is one σ bond and two π bonds. Examples: ethene, CH₂=CH₂, has 5 σ and 1 π; CO₂ has 2 σ and 2 π; N₂ has 1 σ and 2 π; HCN has 2 σ and 2 π.

The mixing of atomic orbitals on an atom to form a new set of equivalent hybrid orbitals used for bonding. The number of hybrid orbitals formed equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed. Hybrid orbitals form σ bonds or hold lone pairs; π bonds form from unhybridized p orbitals.

The hybridization of an atom matches its number of electron domains. Two domains: sp (one s + one p), linear, 180°, two unhybridized p orbitals left (C in CO₂, C and N in HCN). Three domains: sp² (one s + two p), trigonal planar, 120°, one p orbital left (B in BF₃, C in ethene). Four domains: sp³ (one s + three p), tetrahedral, 109.5° (C in CH₄, N in NH₃, O in H₂O, with lone pairs in hybrid orbitals).

mcqs.q: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?
options: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms
The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions H⁺ and Cl⁻
mcqs.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
mcqs.explain: The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both of them. This electrostatic attraction holds the two atoms together, and it is what a covalent bond is.
rationales: Sharing does give each atom a full outer shell, but a 'need' is not a force and cannot hold atoms together. The octet rule describes a tendency; the bond itself is the attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei.
The shared pair is not a rod or hook. It holds the atoms together only because both nuclei are electrostatically attracted to it; the bond is that attraction.
The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both of them. This electrostatic attraction holds the two atoms together, and it is what a covalent bond is.
HCl molecules contain no ions. The H–Cl bond is polar, with partial charges δ+ and δ−, but the electrons are shared. H⁺ and Cl⁻ form only when HCl reacts with water.

mcqs.q: Boron trichloride, BCl₃, is a covalent molecule (boron is in group 13; chlorine is in group 17). In its Lewis formula, how many electrons are in the valence shell of the boron atom?
options: 6 electrons, as boron forms three bonding pairs and has no lone pair
8 electrons, as one B–Cl bond must be a double bond to give boron an octet
3 electrons, as boron has three valence electrons of its own
2 electrons, as boron transfers three electrons to chlorine, leaving 1s²
mcqs.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
mcqs.explain: Each of boron's three valence electrons pairs with one from a chlorine atom, giving three B–Cl bonding pairs and no lone pair: 3 × 2 = 6 electrons, fewer than an octet. Each Cl has one bonding pair and three lone pairs, eight electrons.
mcqs.working: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms one single bond to each Cl atom: 3 bonding pairs × 2 = 6 electrons, with no lone pair left. (Check: total valence electrons 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 = 3 bonding pairs (6) + 9 lone pairs on Cl (18).) Boron has 6 electrons, an incomplete octet.
rationales: Each of boron's three valence electrons pairs with one from a chlorine atom, giving three B–Cl bonding pairs and no lone pair: 3 × 2 = 6 electrons, fewer than an octet. Each Cl has one bonding pair and three lone pairs, eight electrons.
Boron has only three valence electrons, all used in three single B–Cl bonds. The octet rule describes a tendency, not a law: in BCl₃ boron has six electrons, an incomplete octet.
Three is the number of valence electrons of a free boron atom. In the molecule each one is paired with an electron from chlorine, and both electrons of every shared pair count for boron: 3 × 2 = 6.
BCl₃ is a covalent molecule with no ions. Treating it as B³⁺ and Cl⁻ leaves boron with only its 1s² electrons, but boron shares three bonding pairs and has six electrons in its valence shell.

mcqs.q: How does the carbon–carbon bond in ethyne, HC≡CH, compare with the carbon–carbon bond in ethane, CH₃CH₃?
options: It is longer and stronger
It is shorter and weaker
It is longer and weaker
It is shorter and stronger
mcqs.specStatementText: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
mcqs.explain: A triple bond has three shared pairs between the nuclei, against one in the single bond. More shared electrons attract both nuclei more strongly, pulling them closer (C≡C 120 pm, C–C 154 pm) and making the bond harder to break (839 against 346 kJ mol⁻¹).
rationales: The triple bond is stronger, but it is shorter, not longer. The extra shared electrons do not take up extra space between the atoms; they attract both nuclei and pull them closer together (120 pm against 154 pm).

The triple bond is shorter, but it is also stronger overall (839 against 346 kJ mol⁻¹). Alkynes react readily because addition breaks only part of the multiple bond: converting C≡C into C=C needs about 839 − 614 = 225 kJ mol⁻¹, less than a whole C–C bond. The C≡C bond as a whole is not weak.

The shared pairs do repel one another, but their attraction to both nuclei is the larger effect. The triple bond is shorter (120 pm) and stronger (839 kJ mol⁻¹) than the single bond (154 pm, 346 kJ mol⁻¹).

A triple bond has three shared pairs between the nuclei, against one in the single bond. More shared electrons attract both nuclei more strongly, pulling them closer (C≡C 120 pm, C–C 154 pm) and making the bond harder to break (839 against 346 kJ mol⁻¹).

mcqs.q: In the vapour at lower temperatures, aluminium chloride exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules, formed when two AlCl₃ units join through two bridging chlorine atoms. Which describes the new bonds that join the two units?
options: A lone pair on the aluminium atom of each unit is donated to a chlorine atom of the other unit
A lone pair on a chlorine atom of each unit is donated to the aluminium atom of the other
Al³⁺ ions in one unit attract Cl⁻ ions in the other unit, forming two ionic bonds
Each new bond forms from one electron of an aluminium atom and one of a chlorine atom
mcqs.specStatementText: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
mcqs.explain: In AlCl₃, aluminium uses all three valence electrons in bonds and has only six electrons, so it can accept a pair. A chlorine atom of the other unit has lone pairs and donates one, forming a coordination bond. Two such bonds join the units.
rationales: The aluminium atom in AlCl₃ has no lone pair: its three valence electrons are all in Al–Cl bonds. It is the acceptor. The donor is chlorine, which has three lone pairs.

In AlCl₃, aluminium uses all three valence electrons in bonds and has only six electrons, so it can accept a pair. A chlorine atom of the other unit has lone pairs and donates one, forming a coordination bond. Two such bonds join the units.
Aluminium chloride vapour consists of molecules, not ions: the Al–Cl bonds are covalent. The metal/non-metal rule for ionic bonding has exceptions, and aluminium chloride is one.

An aluminium atom in AlCl₃ has no unshared electron left to contribute, because all three of its valence electrons are already in Al–Cl bonds. Both electrons of each new bond must therefore come from chlorine.

mcqs.q: Ammonia, NH₃, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around the nitrogen atom. What is its molecular geometry?
options: Tetrahedral, as there are four electron domains around the nitrogen atom
Trigonal planar, as only the three bonding pairs repel one another
Flat, with 90° bond angles, as the atoms are drawn in its Lewis formula on paper
Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair occupies one of four tetrahedral domains
mcqs.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
mcqs.explain: The four electron domains take up a tetrahedral arrangement (electron-domain geometry). Only three are occupied by atoms, so the atoms form a pyramid with N at the apex: trigonal pyramidal, with H–N–H angles of about 107°.
rationales: Tetrahedral is the electron-domain geometry, which includes the lone pair. The molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms, and with three H atoms around N it is trigonal pyramidal.

The lone pair is an electron domain and repels the bonding pairs strongly. Four domains around nitrogen give a tetrahedral arrangement, so the three H atoms are pushed below the N atom into a pyramid.
A Lewis formula is drawn flat and does not show angles. In three dimensions the four domains point to the corners of a tetrahedron, so NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal with angles of about 107°.

The four electron domains take up a tetrahedral arrangement (electron-domain geometry). Only three are occupied by atoms, so the atoms form a pyramid with N at the apex: trigonal pyramidal, with H–N–H angles of about 107°.

mcqs.q: Predict the H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule, H₂O.
options: About 104.5°, as lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs do
About 109.5°, as all four electron domains around O repel one another equally
About 180°, as the two bonding pairs get as far apart as possible
About 90°, as the H atoms are drawn at right angles in its Lewis formula
mcqs.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
mcqs.explain: Oxygen has four electron domains (two bonding pairs, two lone pairs) in a tetrahedral arrangement. The two lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the H–O–H angle below 109.5° to about 104.5°.
rationales: Oxygen has four electron domains (two bonding pairs, two lone pairs) in a tetrahedral arrangement. The two lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the H–O–H angle below 109.5° to about 104.5°.
The four domains are arranged tetrahedrally, but they do not repel equally. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so the angle between the bonding pairs is reduced to about 104.5°.
Oxygen also has two lone pairs, which are electron domains. With four domains the arrangement is tetrahedral, and the molecule is bent, not linear.
The right angle is a feature of how the Lewis formula is drawn on paper. In three dimensions the four domains around oxygen point towards the corners of a tetrahedron, giving about 104.5°.

mcqs.q: In methanal, H₂CO, the carbon atom forms a single bond to each of two hydrogen atoms and a double bond to the oxygen atom. What is the best prediction of the H–C–H bond angle?
options: About 109.5°, as the two bonds of C=O count as two separate electron domains
Slightly less than 120°, as the C=O double bond repels more than a single bond
Exactly 120°, as all three electron domains around carbon repel equally
About 104.5°, as oxygen's two lone pairs push the two C–H bonds together
mcqs.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
mcqs.explain: Carbon has three electron domains (two C–H bonds and the C=O bond), so the arrangement is trigonal planar. The double bond holds more electron density and repels the C–H bonds more strongly, so the H–C–H angle is squeezed slightly below 120° (to about 116°).
rationales: A double bond is ONE electron domain, because both shared pairs occupy the same region between C and O. Carbon therefore has three domains, not four, and the arrangement is trigonal planar.

Carbon has three electron domains (two C–H bonds and the C=O bond), so the arrangement is trigonal planar. The double bond holds more electron density and repels the C–H bonds more strongly, so the H–C–H angle is squeezed slightly below 120° (to about 116°).

The arrangement is trigonal planar, but the domains do not repel equally. The C=O double bond contains more electron density than a C–H bond, so it repels more and the H–C–H angle falls slightly below 120°.
The lone pairs on oxygen belong to oxygen, not to carbon, so they are not electron domains of the carbon atom. Only the three domains around carbon set the angle, which is close to 120°.

mcqs.q: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?
options: O–H
O–F
C–F
P–H
mcqs.specStatementText: Bond polarity results from the difference in electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
mcqs.explain: The electronegativity difference is 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest of the four, so the shared pair is drawn most unequally, towards F.
rationales: O–H is very polar (difference 3.4 − 2.2 = 1.2) and gives hydrogen bonding, but its difference is smaller than that of C–F (1.4). Polarity is set by the electronegativity difference, not by the ability to hydrogen bond.
O and F are the two most electronegative atoms here, but polarity depends on the difference: 4.0 − 3.4 = 0.6. Two strongly attracting atoms share the pair fairly evenly.
The electronegativity difference is 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest of the four, so the shared pair is drawn most unequally, towards F.
P has many more protons than H, but electronegativity does not follow atomic number: both values are 2.2, so the difference is 0 and the bond is essentially non-polar.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, has no net dipole moment (electronegativity: C 2.6, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?
options: Its two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel
Its C=O bonds are non-polar, as the electronegativity difference is below 1.8
It carries no overall charge, so no separation of charge can exist in the molecule
Its carbon atom has no lone pair, and only lone pairs can produce a net dipole
mcqs.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
mcqs.explain: Each C=O bond is polar (difference 0.8, δ− on O). Carbon has two electron domains, so the molecule is linear and the two equal bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions. Their vector sum is zero.
rationales: Each C=O bond is polar (difference 0.8, δ− on O). Carbon has two electron domains, so the molecule is linear and the two equal bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions. Their vector sum is zero.
Any electronegativity difference makes a bond polar. A difference of 0.8 gives a clearly polar C=O bond; values near 1.8 are only a rough guide to where bonding becomes mainly ionic.
Many neutral molecules have a net dipole, for example H₂O. A dipole is a separation of partial charges within a neutral molecule. CO₂ has none because its bond dipoles cancel.

Lone pairs matter only through their effect on shape. A molecule without a lone pair on its central atom can still be polar (CH₃Cl). CO₂ is non-polar because it is linear and its equal bond dipoles cancel.

mcqs.q: Water, H₂O, has a net dipole moment (electronegativity: H 2.2, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?
options: Its O–H bonds are polar, and every molecule with polar bonds has a net dipole
It is bent, so its two O–H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions
Its H atoms lie at 90° to each other, as in its Lewis formula, so the dipoles add
Its oxygen atom has two lone pairs, which are the only source of its net dipole
mcqs.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
mcqs.explain: Each O–H bond is polar (δ− on O). Oxygen's four electron domains (two of them lone pairs) make the molecule bent, about 104.5°, so the two bond dipoles add to give a resultant along the bisector of the angle.
rationales: The bonds are polar, but polar bonds do not always give a polar molecule: in CO₂ and CCl₄ they cancel. Water is polar because its bent geometry prevents the dipoles from cancelling.

Each O–H bond is polar (δ− on O). Oxygen's four electron domains (two of them lone pairs) make the molecule bent, about 104.5°, so the two bond dipoles add to give a resultant along the bisector of the angle.
The angle is about 104.5°, not 90°. The Lewis formula is drawn flat and does not show angles; VSEPR predicts the bent shape in three dimensions.
The net dipole comes from the polar O–H bonds, which do not cancel. The lone pairs matter because they make the molecule bent; they are not on their own the source of the dipole.

mcqs.q: Graphite conducts electricity. Which feature of its structure explains this?
options: It contains carbon ions that move through the layers when a voltage is applied
Its atoms are held by metallic bonding, as its shiny grey appearance suggests
Each carbon atom bonds to three others, leaving one electron per atom delocalized
Its layers slide over one another easily, carrying electric charge as they move
mcqs.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
mcqs.explain: In each layer every carbon atom forms three covalent bonds. Its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer, and these mobile electrons carry the current along the layers.
rationales: Graphite contains only covalently bonded carbon atoms, not ions. The mobile charged particles are delocalized electrons within each layer.

Graphite looks metallic but is a covalent network: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others. Its conduction comes from electrons delocalized within the covalent layers, not from metallic bonding.
In each layer every carbon atom forms three covalent bonds. Its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer, and these mobile electrons carry the current along the layers.
Sliding layers explain why graphite is soft and slippery; they are held only by weak London forces. Conduction comes from the delocalized electrons within each layer.

mcqs.q: Which statement about carbon allotropes or silicon is correct?
options: Diamond has a very high melting point because of strong intermolecular forces
C₆₀ fullerene is a giant covalent network, so like diamond it dissolves in no solvent
Silicon conducts electricity because its atoms are held together by metallic bonding
Graphene conducts electricity as each atom bonds to three others, leaving delocalized electrons
mcqs.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
mcqs.explain: Graphene is a single layer of graphite: each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds in hexagonal rings, and its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer, so the layer conducts electricity.
rationales: Diamond has no separate molecules, so there are no intermolecular forces to overcome. Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others, and melting requires these strong covalent bonds to be broken.

C₆₀ is a molecular allotrope: separate cage-shaped molecules held together by London forces. It dissolves in non-polar solvents such as methylbenzene and sublimes at a much lower temperature than diamond.
Silicon has a diamond-like covalent network in which each atom is bonded to four others. It is a semiconductor, not a metal, and has no metallic bonding.

Graphene is a single layer of graphite: each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds in hexagonal rings, and its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer, so the layer conducts electricity.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide sublimes at −78 °C, but silicon dioxide melts at about 1700 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
options: Subliming CO₂ breaks its C=O bonds, which are weaker than the Si–O bonds in SiO₂
SiO₂ molecules are heavier than CO₂ molecules, so their London forces are stronger
SiO₂ is a giant covalent network, but CO₂ is made of small separate molecules
SiO₂ is an ionic solid of Si⁴⁺ and O²⁻ ions, like other oxides with high melting points
mcqs.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
mcqs.explain: In SiO₂ each Si atom is covalently bonded to four O atoms and each O atom to two Si atoms, so melting breaks many strong covalent bonds. CO₂ is made of separate molecules, and subliming it overcomes only weak London forces between them.
rationales: Subliming CO₂ does not break any covalent bonds: the vapour consists of intact CO₂ molecules. Only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome. In fact a C=O bond (804 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger than an Si–O bond (466 kJ mol⁻¹); SiO₂ melts far higher because melting it breaks many Si–O bonds, while subliming CO₂ breaks none.
There are no SiO₂ molecules. Silicon dioxide is a covalent network, and the difference of about 1800 °C is far too large to come from a small difference in London forces.

In SiO₂ each Si atom is covalently bonded to four O atoms and each O atom to two Si atoms, so melting breaks many strong covalent bonds. CO₂ is made of separate molecules, and subliming it overcomes only weak London forces between them.
A high melting point does not show ionic bonding. SiO₂ is a covalent network in which each Si atom shares electrons with four O atoms; it contains no ions.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen chloride gas is mixed with iodine vapour. Which intermolecular forces act between an HCl molecule and an I₂ molecule?
options: London forces only, as I₂ is a non-polar molecule with no dipole
London and dipole–induced dipole forces, as HCl polarizes the I₂ molecule
London and dipole–dipole forces, as the HCl molecules are polar
London forces and hydrogen bonds, as HCl has H bonded to electronegative Cl
mcqs.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explain: London forces act between all molecules. HCl also has a permanent dipole, which induces a temporary dipole in the non-polar I₂ molecule, giving a dipole–induced dipole attraction.
rationales: I₂ has no permanent dipole, but the permanent dipole of HCl can induce one in it. So dipole–induced dipole forces act as well as London forces.
London forces act between all molecules. HCl also has a permanent dipole, which induces a temporary dipole in the non-polar I₂ molecule, giving a dipole–induced dipole attraction.
Dipole–dipole forces need a permanent dipole on both molecules. I₂ is non-polar, so the force between HCl and I₂ is dipole–induced dipole, not dipole–dipole.

Cl is electronegative, but hydrogen bonds need H bonded to N, O or F and an N, O or F atom with a lone pair on the other molecule; HCl and I₂ provide neither. The permanent dipole of HCl induces a dipole in I₂, so dipole–induced dipole forces act alongside London forces.

mcqs.q: Liquid methanol, CH₃OH, contains hydrogen bonds. What is a hydrogen bond in methanol?
options: An attraction between the H of an O–H group and a lone pair on O in another molecule
The covalent bond between the O atom and the H atom within one methanol molecule
An attraction between the H atoms of one molecule and the H atoms of another
An attraction between an H atom of the CH₃ group and an O atom in a neighbouring molecule
mcqs.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explain: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen, covalently bonded to an electronegative atom (here O), is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom (O) of a neighbouring molecule.
rationales: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen, covalently bonded to an electronegative atom (here O), is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom (O) of a neighbouring molecule.
That is a covalent bond inside the molecule. A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between the δ+ H of one molecule and an O atom of another.
Hydrogen atoms bonded to O are δ+, so two of them repel. A hydrogen bond links an H atom to an electronegative atom with a lone pair.
Only an H atom bonded to N, O or F takes part. The H atoms of the CH₃ group are bonded to carbon and are not δ+ enough to form hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the intermolecular forces between molecules of propanone, CH₃COCH₃, is correct?
options: They include hydrogen bonds, as each propanone molecule contains H and O atoms
They include no London forces, as propanone molecules are polar
They include London forces, which are the only kind of van der Waals force
They include dipole–dipole forces, which count as van der Waals forces
mcqs.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explain: Propanone is polar: the C=O bond is polar and the bond dipoles do not cancel. So dipole–dipole forces act between its molecules, alongside London forces, and both are included in the term van der Waals forces.
rationales: All the H atoms in propanone are bonded to carbon, so none can form hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules. Hydrogen bonding needs an H atom bonded to N, O or F.
London forces act between all molecules, including polar ones. Propanone has London forces as well as dipole–dipole forces.
London forces are present, but they are not the only kind of van der Waals force. The term includes London, dipole–induced dipole and dipole–dipole forces.

Propanone is polar: the C=O bond is polar and the bond dipoles do not cancel. So dipole–dipole forces act between its molecules, alongside London forces, and both are included in the term van der Waals forces.

mcqs.q: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃ (M_r 44.11), ethanal, CH₃CHO (M_r 44.06), and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (M_r 46.08), have comparable molar masses. Which lists them in order of increasing boiling point?
options: propane < ethanal < ethanol
propane < ethanol < ethanal
ethanal < propane < ethanol
ethanal < ethanol < propane
mcqs.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explain: With comparable molar masses the type of intermolecular force decides. Propane has only London forces (−42 °C); ethanal is polar and adds dipole–dipole forces (20 °C); ethanol forms hydrogen bonds (78 °C).
rationales: With comparable molar masses the type of intermolecular force decides. Propane has only London forces (−42 °C); ethanal is polar and adds dipole–dipole forces (20 °C); ethanol forms hydrogen bonds (78 °C).

Boiling does not break the covalent bonds (such as C=O) inside the molecules; it overcomes the forces between molecules. Ethanol's hydrogen bonding is stronger than ethanal's dipole–dipole forces, so ethanol boils higher.
Ranking by M_r puts ethanal (44.06) below propane (44.11), but the difference is tiny. Ethanal's dipole–dipole forces are stronger than propane's London forces, so it boils at 20 °C against −42 °C.

Boiling point rises with chain length within one homologous series, but these compounds belong to different series. Propane, with only London forces, boils lowest (−42 °C) despite its three carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Which of the following conducts electricity?
options: Liquid sulfur
Diamond crystal
Solid graphite
Ethanol in water
mcqs.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explain: In graphite each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others, and its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer. These mobile electrons carry a current.
rationales: Liquid sulfur consists of neutral S₈ molecules with their electrons held in localized bonds and lone pairs. Melting lets the molecules move, but they carry no charge, so there is no current. Molten ionic compounds conduct because their ions become mobile; molecular substances do not.
Diamond and graphite are both carbon, but their structures differ. In diamond every valence electron is used in four localized C–C bonds, so there are no mobile electrons and it does not conduct.
In graphite each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others, and its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer. These mobile electrons carry a current.
Ethanol dissolves as intact molecules, held among water molecules by hydrogen bonds. It does not ionize, so the solution contains no mobile ions and does not conduct.

mcqs.q: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane, C₆H₁₄, does not dissolve in water. Which statement explains this difference?
options: Ethanol splits into ions that water surrounds, but hexane does not form ions
Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane cannot
Hexane is less dense than water, so it floats on the water rather than dissolving
Hexane molecules are too large to fit into the gaps between water molecules
mcqs.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explain: The O–H group of ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water, replacing the hydrogen bonds broken between water molecules. Hexane forms only London forces with water, far weaker than the hydrogen bonds it would have to break, so it does not dissolve.
rationales: Ethanol dissolves as intact molecules; its solution does not conduct electricity. It dissolves because it forms hydrogen bonds with water, not because it ionizes.

The O–H group of ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water, replacing the hydrogen bonds broken between water molecules. Hexane forms only London forces with water, far weaker than the hydrogen bonds it would have to break, so it does not dissolve.
Density decides which layer floats once two liquids fail to mix, not whether they mix. Ethanol is also less dense than water, yet it mixes completely.

Solubility depends on the attractions formed between solute and solvent, not on fitting into gaps. Sucrose molecules are larger than hexane molecules but dissolve readily because they hydrogen bond with water.

mcqs.q: In a paper chromatography experiment the baseline was drawn 1.0 cm above the bottom edge of the paper. At the end, the solvent front was 11.0 cm above the bottom edge and the centre of a spot was 4.4 cm above the bottom edge. What is the RF value of the spot?
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
mcqs.explain: Distance moved by the spot = 4.4 − 1.0 = 3.4 cm; distance moved by the solvent = 11.0 − 1.0 = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
mcqs.working: Distance moved by spot = 4.4 cm − 1.0 cm = 3.4 cm. Distance moved by solvent = 11.0 cm − 1.0 cm = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 cm ÷ 10.0 cm = 0.34 (no units).
rationales: This is 10.0 ÷ 3.4, the solvent distance divided by the spot distance. RF is the spot distance divided by the solvent distance, so it can never exceed 1.
This is 4.4 ÷ 11.0, with both distances measured from the bottom edge of the paper. The spot and solvent both started from the baseline, so measure from there: 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
This is (11.0 − 4.4) ÷ 10.0, the gap between the spot and the solvent front. Despite the name 'retardation factor', RF uses the distance the spot moved from the baseline: 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
Distance moved by the spot = 4.4 − 1.0 = 3.4 cm; distance moved by the solvent = 11.0 − 1.0 = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.

mcqs.q: A mixture is separated by paper chromatography. Under the same conditions, component X has an RF value of 0.20 and component Y has an RF value of 0.75. Which statement is correct?
options: Relative to the mobile phase, X is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase than Y is
X has larger molecules than Y, so the fibres of the paper hold X back more than Y
X would also reach an RF of 0.75 if the solvent were allowed to run for a longer time
X is less soluble in the solvent than Y, and the paper plays no part in the separation
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
mcqs.explain: A component moves more slowly when it is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase relative to the mobile phase. X travels only 0.20 of the solvent's distance, so this balance favours the stationary phase more for X than for Y.
rationales: A component moves more slowly when it is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase relative to the mobile phase. X travels only 0.20 of the solvent's distance, so this balance favours the stationary phase more for X than for Y.
The paper is not a sieve. Separation depends on the relative attractions of each component to the stationary and mobile phases, not on molecular size.
Running longer increases both the spot's distance and the solvent's distance in proportion, so X's RF stays 0.20. That is why RF values can be used to identify components.
The stationary phase is half of the separation. RF depends on the balance of attractions to both phases, so the paper's attraction for each component matters as much as solubility in the solvent.

mcqs.q: Ozone, O₃, can be represented by two Lewis formulas that differ only in which O–O bond is shown as the double bond. Which describes the bonds in a real ozone molecule?
options: One single and one double bond, fixed in place exactly as one of the two Lewis formulas shows
Two identical bonds, intermediate between single and double, as electrons are delocalized
Two double bonds, with the central oxygen atom expanding its octet to ten electrons
One single and one double bond, which swap positions rapidly back and forth
mcqs.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
mcqs.explain: The real molecule is a resonance hybrid. The electrons of the 'double bond' are delocalized over all three atoms, so both O–O bonds are identical and intermediate in length and strength between O–O and O=O.
rationales: No single Lewis formula is the real structure. Both O–O bonds in ozone are measured to be the same length, which neither resonance structure shows on its own.

The real molecule is a resonance hybrid. The electrons of the 'double bond' are delocalized over all three atoms, so both O–O bonds are identical and intermediate in length and strength between O–O and O=O.
Oxygen is in period 2 and cannot expand its octet. The equal bonds arise from delocalization, not from two double bonds.
The molecule does not switch between structures. It has one structure at all times, with delocalized electrons and two identical bonds.

mcqs.q: In the ethanoate ion, CH₃COO⁻, the carbon atom of the COO group is bonded to the CH₃ carbon and to both O atoms. How many resonance structures can be deduced for the ethanoate ion?
options: 0 structures, as the atoms bonded to the central C are not all the same
3 structures, as C can also form double bonds to both O atoms at once
2 structures, as the C=O double bond can be drawn to either O atom
4 structures, as an H atom can also move from CH₃ onto either O atom
mcqs.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
mcqs.explain: The COO carbon is bonded to CH₃ and to two equivalent O atoms. The C=O double bond can be drawn to either O, with the −1 charge on the other, giving two resonance structures that differ only in the position of the double bond; the real ion is their hybrid, with two identical C–O bonds.
mcqs.working: Valence electrons: 2 × C 4 + 3 × H 1 + 2 × O 6 + 1 (charge) = 24. The Lewis formula has three C–H bonds, a C–C bond, one C=O double bond and one C–O single bond, the singly bonded O carrying the −1 formal charge. The two O atoms are equivalent, so the double bond can be drawn to either of them: 2 resonance structures. A double bond to both O atoms would give carbon ten electrons (not possible in period 2), and moving an H atom changes the positions of atoms, giving a different species.
rationales: Resonance needs more than one possible position for a double bond, not identical atoms all round the carbon. The two O atoms are equivalent, so the C=O bond can be drawn to either of them: two structures.
A double bond to both O atoms would give carbon ten electrons. Carbon is in period 2 and cannot expand its octet, so only the two structures with one C=O bond are valid.

The COO carbon is bonded to CH₃ and to two equivalent O atoms. The C=O double bond can be drawn to either O, with the −1 charge on the other, giving two resonance structures that differ only in the position of the double bond; the real ion is their hybrid, with two identical C–O bonds.
Moving an H atom changes the positions of atoms and gives a different species, not a resonance structure. Resonance structures differ only in the positions of electrons: here there are two.

mcqs.q: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene (one C=C bond) is about −120 kJ mol⁻¹. For benzene, forming cyclohexane, it is about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, much less exothermic than the −360 kJ mol⁻¹ predicted for a structure with three localized C=C bonds. Which statement explains the difference?
options: Breaking benzene's delocalized bonds releases less energy than breaking three C=C bonds
Benzene has only one or two C=C bonds, since 208 lies between 1 × 120 and 2 × 120
Benzene reacts incompletely with hydrogen, so less energy is released per mole
Delocalization lowers benzene's energy, so less energy is released as it is hydrogenated
mcqs.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
mcqs.explain: Benzene and the hypothetical three-C=C structure give the same product, cyclohexane. Benzene starts about 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ lower in energy because its π electrons are delocalized, so less energy is released.
rationales: Breaking bonds absorbs energy; it never releases it. The energy released comes from bonds formed. Benzene releases less because it starts at a lower energy.

Benzene adds three moles of H₂ to form cyclohexane (C₆H₆ → C₆H₁₂), which a ring with only one or two C=C bonds could not do, and all six of its C–C bonds are identical. ΔH is not simply proportional to the number of double bonds: delocalization lowers benzene's energy, so it releases less than 3 × 120 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH is quoted per mole of reaction as written (C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂) and does not depend on how much reacts in an experiment. The smaller value reflects benzene's extra stability.

Benzene and the hypothetical three-C=C structure give the same product, cyclohexane. Benzene starts about 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ lower in energy because its π electrons are delocalized, so less energy is released.

mcqs.q: Cyclohexene reacts with bromine by addition. Benzene reacts with bromine only in the presence of a catalyst, and then by substitution, forming C₆H₅Br and HBr. Which statement explains why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition?
options: Benzene has no π electrons at all, so like an alkane it can only take part in substitution
Substitution leaves benzene's delocalized ring of π electrons, and its stability, intact
Benzene contains three C=C bonds that are far stronger than the C=C bond in cyclohexene itself
Benzene's C=C bonds move around the ring too quickly for bromine to add across them
mcqs.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
mcqs.explain: Addition would destroy the delocalized π system and lose its stabilization of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹. Substitution replaces an H atom and keeps the delocalized ring, so it is favoured.
rationales: Benzene does have π electrons: six of them, delocalized around the ring. It is unsaturated and adds hydrogen to form cyclohexane. It favours substitution because this keeps the delocalized system.
Addition would destroy the delocalized π system and lose its stabilization of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹. Substitution replaces an H atom and keeps the delocalized ring, so it is favoured.

Benzene has no localized C=C bonds: all six C–C bonds are identical (about 140 pm). Its stability belongs to the delocalized π system as a whole, not to strong individual double bonds, and substitution keeps that system intact.
The π electrons are delocalized at all times; no double bonds move around the ring. The stability of the delocalized system is what makes substitution favourable.

mcqs.q: In sulfur tetrafluoride, SF₄, the sulfur atom (six valence electrons) forms a single bond to each of four fluorine atoms. What is the molecular geometry of SF₄?
options: Tetrahedral, as only the four bonding pairs repel one another around sulfur
Trigonal bipyramidal, as there are five electron domains around the sulfur atom
Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair takes an axial site in a trigonal bipyramid
See-saw, as the lone pair takes an equatorial site in a trigonal bipyramid
mcqs.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
mcqs.explain: Sulfur uses four of its six valence electrons in bonds and keeps one lone pair: five electron domains, trigonal bipyramidal. The lone pair takes an equatorial position (fewer 90° repulsions), leaving the four F atoms in a see-saw shape.
rationales: Sulfur also has a lone pair, which is an electron domain and must be counted. With five domains the arrangement is trigonal bipyramidal, not tetrahedral.
Trigonal bipyramidal is the electron-domain geometry, which includes the lone pair. The molecular geometry describes the atoms only: see-saw.
An axial lone pair would have three neighbours at 90°; an equatorial one has only two, so the lone pair goes equatorial. The shape is see-saw.

Sulfur uses four of its six valence electrons in bonds and keeps one lone pair: five electron domains, trigonal bipyramidal. The lone pair takes an equatorial position (fewer 90° repulsions), leaving the four F atoms in a see-saw shape.

mcqs.q: In xenon tetrafluoride, XeF₄, the xenon atom (eight valence electrons) forms a single bond to each of four fluorine atoms. What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
options: Tetrahedral, as only its four bonding pairs repel one another around the Xe atom
Octahedral, as there are six electron domains around the xenon atom
Square planar, as the two lone pairs occupy opposite positions of an octahedron
See-saw, as the two lone pairs occupy adjacent positions, 90° apart, in an octahedron
mcqs.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
mcqs.explain: Xenon uses four electrons in bonds and keeps two lone pairs: six electron domains, octahedral. The two lone pairs repel most strongly, so they sit opposite each other, leaving the four F atoms in a square plane.
rationales: Xenon also has two lone pairs, giving six electron domains in an octahedral arrangement. Ignoring the lone pairs gives the wrong shape.
Octahedral is the electron-domain geometry, including the two lone pairs. The atoms alone form a square plane.

Xenon uses four electrons in bonds and keeps two lone pairs: six electron domains, octahedral. The two lone pairs repel most strongly, so they sit opposite each other, leaving the four F atoms in a square plane.
Two lone pairs 90° apart would repel strongly. They take opposite positions, 180° apart, so XeF₄ is square planar.

mcqs.q: In the Lewis formula of carbon monoxide, C and O are joined by a triple bond and each atom has one lone pair. Using FC = V − N − ½B (V = valence electrons of the free atom, N = non-bonding electrons, B = bonding electrons), what is the formal charge on the carbon atom?
mcqs.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
mcqs.explain: V = 4, N = 2 (one lone pair), B = 6 (three shared pairs). FC = 4 − 2 − ½ × 6 = −1.
mcqs.working: Carbon: V = 4; N = 2 (one lone pair); B = 6 (triple bond). FC = V − N − ½B = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1. (Oxygen: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; the sum, 0, equals the charge of the molecule.)
rationales: V = 4, N = 2 (one lone pair), B = 6 (three shared pairs). FC = 4 − 2 − ½ × 6 = −1.
This is N + ½B − V = 2 + 3 − 4, the subtraction reversed. FC = V − N − ½B = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1.
This is 4 − 2 − 6, subtracting all six bonding electrons. Each shared pair is split equally between the two atoms, so only half, 3, is subtracted: FC = −1.
+2 is the oxidation state of carbon in CO, found by giving all the bonding electrons to oxygen. Formal charge shares them equally: FC = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1.

mcqs.q: Two Lewis formulas are proposed for CO₂. In formula I, each O atom is joined to C by a double bond and has two lone pairs. In formula II, one O atom is joined to C by a triple bond and has one lone pair, and the other O atom is joined by a single bond and has three lone pairs. Which formula is preferred, and why?
options: Formula I, as the sum of all its formal charges is zero
Formula II, as it places a negative formal charge on an oxygen atom
Formula II, as its triple bond is stronger than any double bond
Formula I, as every atom in it has a formal charge of zero
mcqs.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
mcqs.explain: Formula I: C 4 − 0 − 4 = 0; each O 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Formula II: triple-bonded O 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, C 0, single-bonded O 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Formula I has formal charges closest to zero, so it is preferred.
rationales: The formal charges in formula I do add up to zero, but so do those in formula II (+1, 0 and −1): every valid formula for a neutral molecule sums to zero. The sum is only a check. Formula I is preferred because each atom's formal charge is zero, the values closest to zero.
Placing negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom is only a tie-breaker. The first criterion is formal charges as close to zero as possible, which favours formula I.
Formula II has a stronger C≡O bond but a weaker C–O bond as well; the preference is decided by formal charge, which favours formula I (all zero).
Formula I: C 4 − 0 − 4 = 0; each O 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Formula II: triple-bonded O 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, C 0, single-bonded O 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Formula I has formal charges closest to zero, so it is preferred.

mcqs.q: How many σ (sigma) bonds are there in one molecule of propenenitrile, CH₂=CH–C≡N?
mcqs.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
mcqs.explain: Three C–H bonds (3 σ), the C=C bond (1 σ + 1 π), the C–C bond (1 σ) and the C≡N bond (1 σ + 2 π): 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 σ bonds (and 3 π bonds).
mcqs.working: σ bonds: C–H × 3 = 3; C=C contributes 1 σ; C–C contributes 1 σ; C≡N contributes 1 σ. Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 σ bonds (π bonds: 1 in C=C + 2 in C≡N = 3).
rationales: 9 is the total number of shared pairs (6 σ + 3 π). Only one bond between each pair of atoms is a σ bond; the extra bonds in C=C and C≡N are π bonds.
This counts only the single bonds (3 C–H + 1 C–C) as σ. Every multiple bond also contains one σ bond, so C=C and C≡N add one σ each: 6.
Three C–H bonds (3 σ), the C=C bond (1 σ + 1 π), the C–C bond (1 σ) and the C≡N bond (1 σ + 2 π): 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 σ bonds (and 3 π bonds).
This counts the C≡N triple bond as two σ bonds. A triple bond is one σ bond and two π bonds, so the total is 6.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide has the Lewis formula O=C=O. How many σ and π bonds does one CO₂ molecule contain?
options: Four σ bonds and zero π bonds
Two σ bonds and two π bonds
No σ bond and four π bonds
Two σ bonds and no π bond
mcqs.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
mcqs.explain: Each C=O double bond is one σ bond (head-on overlap along the axis) and one π bond (lateral overlap of p orbitals). Two double bonds give 2 σ and 2 π.
rationales: Only one bond between each pair of atoms can be σ. The second bond of each C=O is a π bond, so CO₂ has 2 σ and 2 π.
Each C=O double bond is one σ bond (head-on overlap along the axis) and one π bond (lateral overlap of p orbitals). Two double bonds give 2 σ and 2 π.
Every double bond contains one σ bond along the bond axis; a π bond only forms between atoms already joined by a σ bond. CO₂ has 2 σ and 2 π.
Each C=O is two shared pairs, not one. The first is a σ bond and the second a π bond, so CO₂ has 2 σ and 2 π.

mcqs.q: In ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, the nitrogen atom is joined to carbon by a triple bond and carries one lone pair. What is the hybridization of the nitrogen atom?
options: sp, as it has two electron domains: the triple bond and the lone pair
sp², as it forms three bonds to the carbon atom, one for each shared pair
sp³, as nitrogen is sp³ hybridized in ammonia and keeps that in its compounds
Not hybridized, as only carbon atoms form hybrid orbitals in molecules
mcqs.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
mcqs.explain: The triple bond counts as one electron domain and the lone pair as another. Two domains correspond to sp hybridization, with the domains at 180°; the two unhybridized p orbitals form the two π bonds.
rationales: The triple bond counts as one electron domain and the lone pair as another. Two domains correspond to sp hybridization, with the domains at 180°; the two unhybridized p orbitals form the two π bonds.
Hybridization follows the number of electron domains, not the number of bonds. The triple bond is one domain, and two of its bonds are π bonds, which use unhybridized p orbitals.
Hybridization depends on the domains around the atom in each species. In NH₃ nitrogen has four domains (sp³); in CH₃CN it has two (sp).
Any atom's bonding can be described by hybridization. Nitrogen here has two electron domains and is sp hybridized.

mcqs.q: Which statement about hybridization in an inorganic species is correct?
options: The nitrogen atom in NH₃ is not hybridized, as only carbon forms hybrid orbitals
The carbon atom in CO₂ is sp³ hybridized, as it forms 4 bonds in total
The carbon atom in HCN forms its two π bonds from sp hybrid orbitals
The boron atom in BF₃ is sp² hybridized, with its three hybrid orbitals at 120°
mcqs.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
mcqs.explain: Boron has three electron domains (three B–F bonds, no lone pair), so it is sp² hybridized and the three hybrid orbitals lie in a plane at 120°, giving the trigonal planar shape.
rationales: Nitrogen in NH₃ has four electron domains (three bonding pairs and a lone pair) and is sp³ hybridized, like carbon in CH₄.
Carbon in CO₂ has two electron domains (two double bonds), so it is sp hybridized and linear. Two of its four bonds are π bonds, formed from unhybridized p orbitals.
The sp hybrid orbitals of carbon form its two σ bonds (to H and N). Its two π bonds form from the two unhybridized p orbitals.
Boron has three electron domains (three B–F bonds, no lone pair), so it is sp² hybridized and the three hybrid orbitals lie in a plane at 120°, giving the trigonal planar shape.

mcqs.q: Silicon is a shiny grey solid that melts at 1414 °C, conducts electricity only slightly and does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which describes the structure of solid silicon?
options: A lattice of positive Si ions in a sea of delocalized electrons, as in metals
A network in which each Si atom is covalently bonded to four others, as in diamond
Separate silicon molecules held together by strong intermolecular forces
Flat layers in which each Si atom is bonded to three others, as in graphite
mcqs.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
mcqs.explain: Each Si atom forms four covalent bonds to other Si atoms in a tetrahedral three-dimensional network, as C does in diamond. Melting breaks many strong Si–Si bonds, hence 1414 °C, and no solvent can separate the atoms.
rationales: Silicon looks shiny and conducts a little, but it contains no positive ions in a sea of electrons. It is a covalent network, and its slight conductivity is that of a semiconductor, far below that of a metal.

Each Si atom forms four covalent bonds to other Si atoms in a tetrahedral three-dimensional network, as C does in diamond. Melting breaks many strong Si–Si bonds, hence 1414 °C, and no solvent can separate the atoms.
A substance of separate molecules held by intermolecular forces melts far below 1414 °C. Silicon has no molecules: melting it breaks covalent Si–Si bonds, which is why its melting point is so high.
Silicon has no delocalized electron per atom: each Si atom bonds to four others, as in diamond, not three as in graphite. Its slight conductivity comes from its being a semiconductor.

mcqs.q: C₆₀ fullerene dissolves in methylbenzene, but diamond and graphite do not dissolve in any common solvent. Which statement explains the difference?
options: C₆₀ consists of separate molecules held by London forces; diamond and graphite are covalent networks
C₆₀ splits into ions in methylbenzene, but diamond and graphite cannot form ions
Diamond and graphite are held together by strong intermolecular forces between their atoms
Methylbenzene breaks the C–C bonds in C₆₀, which are weaker than those in diamond
mcqs.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
mcqs.explain: C₆₀ is a molecular allotrope: methylbenzene molecules can surround separate C₆₀ molecules, overcoming only the London forces between them. Diamond and graphite are covalent networks; dissolving them would mean breaking strong C–C covalent bonds.
rationales: C₆₀ is a molecular allotrope: methylbenzene molecules can surround separate C₆₀ molecules, overcoming only the London forces between them. Diamond and graphite are covalent networks; dissolving them would mean breaking strong C–C covalent bonds.
Neither C₆₀ nor methylbenzene forms ions. C₆₀ dissolves as intact molecules, held among the solvent molecules by London forces, and the solution does not conduct.

The atoms of diamond, and the atoms within each graphite layer, are joined by covalent bonds, not intermolecular forces. Neither dissolves because every atom is covalently bonded into a network that a solvent cannot break up.
Dissolving does not break covalent bonds: C₆₀ dissolves as intact C₆₀ molecules. The C–C bonds in all three allotropes are strong; the difference is between separate molecules and covalent networks.

mcqs.q: In methanamine, CH₃NH₂, the nitrogen atom is sp³ hybridized and carries one lone pair. What is the molecular geometry around the nitrogen atom?
options: Tetrahedral, as its four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron
Trigonal planar, as only its three bonding pairs repel one another
Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair fills one of the four sp³ orbitals
Bent, as an sp³ atom with a lone pair is bent, like O in water
mcqs.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
mcqs.explain: The four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron; three hold the bonding pairs to C, H and H and one holds the lone pair. The three atoms around N form a trigonal pyramid, as in NH₃.
rationales: Tetrahedral describes the four sp³ orbitals, including the one holding the lone pair. The geometry is named from the atoms only: three atoms around N form a trigonal pyramid.
An sp³ atom has four electron domains, and the lone pair repels the bonding pairs strongly. Trigonal planar would need sp² with no lone pair; here the three bonds are pushed into a pyramid.
The four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron; three hold the bonding pairs to C, H and H and one holds the lone pair. The three atoms around N form a trigonal pyramid, as in NH₃.
Bent needs two bonded atoms and two lone pairs, as for O in water. N here has three bonded atoms and one lone pair, so the geometry is trigonal pyramidal.

mcqs.q: In the Lewis formula of methanal, H₂CO, the carbon atom is bonded to both H atoms and to the O atom. How many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom?
options: 2 lone pairs, as 4 of the 12 valence electrons remain after the C–H and C=O bonds
4 lone pairs, as O gains two electrons from C and is an O²⁻ ion with an octet
3 lone pairs, as the C=O double bond is one shared pair, so O needs three more
0 lone pairs, as a Lewis formula shows only the bonding pairs between the atoms
mcqs.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
mcqs.explain: Methanal has 4 + 2 × 1 + 6 = 12 valence electrons. Two C–H bonds and a C=O double bond use 8, leaving 4, which form two lone pairs on O. O then has 4 + 4 = 8 electrons and C has 8.
mcqs.working: Valence electrons: C 4 + 2 × H 1 + O 6 = 12. Carbon forms two C–H bonds (4 electrons) and a C=O double bond (4 electrons), 8 electrons in bonds. The remaining 12 − 8 = 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs on O. Check: O has 4 (C=O) + 4 (lone pairs) = 8; C has 2 × 2 + 4 = 8; each H has 2.
rationales: Methanal has 4 + 2 × 1 + 6 = 12 valence electrons. Two C–H bonds and a C=O double bond use 8, leaving 4, which form two lone pairs on O. O then has 4 + 4 = 8 electrons and C has 8.

Methanal is a covalent molecule with no ions. O shares two pairs with C in the C=O double bond and holds two lone pairs: 4 + 4 = 8 electrons. Four lone pairs as well as the C=O bond would give O twelve electrons.
A double bond is two shared pairs, four electrons. O has four electrons from C=O, so two lone pairs complete its octet; three would give it ten and use more electrons than the molecule has.
A Lewis formula shows all the valence electrons, lone pairs included. After the bonds, 4 of methanal's 12 valence electrons remain, as two lone pairs on O.

mcqs.q: The O–O bond in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, has a length of 148 pm; the O=O bond in oxygen, O₂, has a length of 121 pm. Which statement about the strengths of these two bonds is correct?
options: O=O is weaker, as the two shared pairs between the nuclei repel each other strongly
O=O is weaker, as oxygen reacts so readily, for example in combustion reactions
O=O is stronger, as two shared pairs attract both nuclei more than one
The two bonds have the same strength, as both are between two oxygen atoms
mcqs.specStatementText: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
mcqs.explain: Two shared pairs between the nuclei mean more negative charge attracting both nuclei, so they are pulled closer (121 pm against 148 pm) and more energy is needed to separate them: O=O about 498 kJ mol⁻¹ against O–O about 144 kJ mol⁻¹. Shorter and stronger go together.
rationales: The shared pairs do repel one another, but the shorter bond length shows that the attraction of both nuclei for the extra pair is the larger effect. A shorter bond between the same two atoms is a stronger bond: O=O is about 498 kJ mol⁻¹, O–O about 144 kJ mol⁻¹.

Reactivity does not measure bond strength. Combustion releases energy because the C=O and O–H bonds formed are stronger than the bonds broken, not because O=O is weak. The O=O bond (about 498 kJ mol⁻¹) is much stronger than O–O (about 144 kJ mol⁻¹), as its shorter length suggests.

Two shared pairs between the nuclei mean more negative charge attracting both nuclei, so they are pulled closer (121 pm against 148 pm) and more energy is needed to separate them: O=O about 498 kJ mol⁻¹ against O–O about 144 kJ mol⁻¹. Shorter and stronger go together.

The atoms are the same but the number of shared pairs is not. The O=O bond is shorter because two pairs attract the nuclei more strongly, and it is correspondingly stronger: about 498 kJ mol⁻¹ against about 144 kJ mol⁻¹ for O–O.

mcqs.q: Ammonia, NH₃, reacts with a hydrogen ion, H⁺, to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Which statement about the bonds in NH₄⁺ is correct?
options: The bond formed from the lone pair on nitrogen is longer and weaker than the other three N–H bonds
The new bond formed from a pair of electrons supplied by the H⁺ ion to nitrogen
The new bond formed from one electron supplied by nitrogen and one electron supplied by H⁺
All four N–H bonds are identical, although one formed from the lone pair on nitrogen
mcqs.specStatementText: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
mcqs.explain: H⁺ has no electrons, so the new bond is a coordination bond: both electrons come from the lone pair on nitrogen. Once formed, a coordination bond is an ordinary covalent bond, and all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ have the same length and strength.
rationales: Where the electrons came from leaves no trace: electrons are indistinguishable. The arrow sometimes drawn for a coordination bond only records its origin. All four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are equivalent.
A hydrogen ion is a bare proton with no electrons, so it cannot supply a pair. The donor is the atom with the lone pair, nitrogen; H⁺ is the acceptor.

H⁺ has no electron to contribute, and the nitrogen atom in NH₃ has no unpaired electron left, only a lone pair. Both electrons of the new bond come from nitrogen's lone pair: it is a coordination bond.
